###### Abstract
I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers’ effects and from trends in untreated outcomes.
## 1 Introduction
Some units are treated before the policy and start treatment for reasons unrelated to it, while some units are exposed to the policy and remain untreated. The canonical estimator in this setting is the Wald-DiD ratio, which divides the DiD in outcomes by the DiD in treatment rates (Duflo, 2001).
I derive an exact causal decomposition of the design-based Wald-DiD estimand . It equals an assignment-probability-weighted average of complier effects plus three contamination terms: the effects of treatment on switchers, the change over time in the effects of treatment on always-takers, and trends in untreated outcomes. Each term enters the expression through its finite-population covariance with the assignment probabilities.
Second, I characterize the conditions under which the Wald-DiD design estimand equals the weighted complier effect: the assignment probabilities must be uncorrelated with a single contamination index that combines untreated trends, switcher effects and the drift in always-takers’ effects.

## Abstract

I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers’ effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. I derive the conditions under which the estimand holds a clear causal interpretation. The conditions are weaker than parallel trends in both outcomes and treatments. We propose an Anderson–Rubin-type test with a conservative Neyman variance that remains valid under weak first stages, a sensitivity analysis for the complier effect, and estimators for designs with known assignment probabilities. An application to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment illustrates the results.

Globally, multiple river systems are affected by urbanization, agricultural runoff, industrial discharges, and diffuse sources of contamination (Strokal et al., 2019). These overlapping pressures complicate assessment because a single contaminant or source rarely determines the ecological condition of a water body. Consequently, effective water quality evaluation requires integrative approaches that capture the combined effects of diverse stressors and translate complex monitoring data into information that supports decision-making (Schuwirth, 2020).
A comprehensive water quality assessment requires the analysis and interpretation of multiple physical, chemical, and microbiological parameters. While this parameter-based approach provides detailed information, it is often time-consuming, technically demanding, and difficult to communicate clearly to water managers and the broader public (Giri, 2021). Water quality indices (WQIs) were developed to address this challenge by integrating multiple parameters into a single dimensionless score, often expressed on a scale from 0 to 100, that provides an overall indication of water body condition and supports communication with managers and stakeholders (Uddin et al., 2023). octen.title: Specification Limit Normalization for Nonparametric Process Capability Analysis and Its Application in Cleaning Validation with AI-Enabled Monitoring Models | AAPS PharmSciTech | Springer Nature Link
octen.snippet:
Abstract
In pharmaceutical manufacturing, equipment is often used for multiple products following a single standard cleaning process regardless of the previously manufactured product. Despite this, residue levels are frequently non-detectable. Regulatory guidelines, such as the EMA Q&A on HBELs, mandate cleaning and visual inspection after each use, with analytical testing required after product changeovers unless otherwise justified. Consequently, cleaning validation (CV) data is typically left-censored, limited in sample size, and subject to multiple upper specification limits (USLs). These realities limit the applicability of traditional parametric capability indices and reduce the robustness of nonparametric methods. Moreover, they hinder the effective use of historical CV data in AI applications, which depend on large, standardized datasets for model training. To address these challenges, we propose a USL-normalization method that standardizes all residue measurements to a unified USL_Pct = 100. This transformation enables the aggregation of USL-heterogeneous datasets and supports robust nonparametric analysis. The cleaning process CQA (critical quality attribute) level upper capability index Ppu is calculated using the KDEDPonUSLND algorithm (kernel density estimation derived percentiles on USL-normalized data), which demonstrates improved robustness compared to traditional approaches. The cleaning process level Ppu is evaluated using either CQAWWC (CQA-wise worst case) or CQAWP (CQA-wise pooling) strategies, both integrated with the KDEDPonUSLND algorithm. The resulting CQAWWC_BAKEDPonUSLND and CQAWP_BAKEDPonUSLND models support an AI-driven CV Stage 3 Continued Cleaning Process Verification/Monitoring system, aligned with regulatory expectations.

(1)CREST, ENSAE, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91120 Palaiseau, France

Abstract We consider a bivariate contamination model L = (1−p)F0 +pF in which the distribution F0 of a gold standard is known while the mixing weight p and the distribution F of the con-taminant component are unknown, and we test whether the two coordinates of the unknown component are independent, i.e. F = F1 ⊗F2. Classical tests of independence applied to the observed sample are meaningless in this setting, since a mixture of product distributions is not a product distribution. Following the Inversion–Best Matching (IBM) principle, we invert the contamination model for every candidate weight, which yields two parametric families of functions: the inverted cdfs of the unknown component and the products of their marginals. The weight is estimated by the value at which these two families are closest in a Cram´er–von Mises sense, and the empirical minimal distance scaled by n (the sample size) is the test statis-tic. We show that the discrepancy between the two families has an exact quadratic structure in 1/p. The contrast is then a quartic polynomial in 1/p with explicit empirical coefficients, so the weight estimator is obtained exactly, by comparing a finite number of candidates: the roots of a cubic equation and the endpoints of the parameter set.

### Pedro Picchetti ∗

**Abstract**

I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment prob- abilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers’ effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. I derive the conditions under which the estimand holds a clear causal interpretation. The conditions are weaker than parallel trends in both outcomes and treatments. We propose an Anderson–Rubin-type test with a conservative Neyman variance that remains valid under weak first stages, a sensitivity analysis for the complier effect, and estimators for designs with known assignment probabilities. An application to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment illustrates the results.

ultimate.snippet:
I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers’ effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. I derive the conditions under which the estimand holds a clear causal interpretation.

The canonical estimator in this setting is the Wald-DiD ratio, which divides the DiD in outcomes by the DiD in treatment rates (Duflo, 2001). de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2018) showed that, in the conventional sampling-based framework, the Wald-DiD estimand identifies a local average treatment effect only under strong homogeneity restrictions: parallel trends must be combined with stability of treatment effects over time and homogeneity of effects between groups.

Second, I characterize the conditions under which the Wald-DiD design estimand equals the weighted complier effect: the assignment probabilities must be uncorrelated with a single contamination index that combines untreated trends, switcher effects and the drift in always-takers’ effects. This condition is necessary and sufficient, and it is strictly weaker than the pair of orthogonality conditions (design-based parallel trends for outcomes and for treatment) that would follow from applying existing results directly (Hudson et al., 2017; Rambachan and Roth, 2026). For example, it holds under design-based parallel trends and homogeneous effects even when switchers are concentrated among units likely to be assigned.

Oasis cities are located at the edges of deserts, and the frequency and intensity of dust storms are usually higher than those in humid areas, which has a negative impact on urban ecology and residents’ health [62,63,64]. A study of HMs in air dust from a typical oasis city in Iran found that most of the HMs in Zabol air dust had a high bioaccessibility and the associated HMs produced carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic risks for both adults and children that were greater than the safety threshold [65].
